speaker_role: independent counselor (known college essay coach/consultant, referred to by the channel name 'College Essay Guy'; not a former admissions officer)
commercial_incentive: Yes - promotes his paid online essay-writing courses throughout, though he notes refunds and pay-what-you-can options are available
key_insights: Analyzes a real (anonymized) admitted student's personal statement, highlighting techniques like 'geeky language' (using field-specific jargon early to signal genuine subject expertise) and setting up recurring themes (family, curiosity) in the opening lines
Notes the essay works partly because it braids humor with substantive themes (a running motif of 'questioning the unknown') that pays off later in the essay, rather than being purely descriptive

In the activities list, highlights the value of using specific numbers to demonstrate concrete impact rather than vague descriptions, and varying the framing across entries so they don't all sound like restatements of the same activity
Recommends using the Additional Information section to expand on research/volunteer work that didn't fit in the activities list, rather than leaving it unused
Introduces the concept of a 'super essay' - writing 3-5 reusable, flexible essays that can be adapted across multiple schools' supplemental prompts instead of writing dozens of fully unique essays

Uses the student's actual 'Why Dartmouth' essay (built around a 3D-graph metaphor of science/humanities/global understanding) as an example of a short, structurally distinctive supplemental essay that was successfully reused as a template for other schools' prompts

Argues that students should define 'success' in the process based on what they can control (whether the application genuinely demonstrates their skills/values), not solely on which specific school admits them
specific_numbers_or_facts: The featured student was admitted to and ultimately attended Dartmouth
notable_or_distinctive: The 'super essay' concept (reusing a strong essay's structure/content across multiple supplemental prompts, as the featured student did with her Dartmouth and math essays) is a concrete, reusable strategic technique rather than generic essay-writing advice.
reliability_notes: Based on a single real but anonymized applicant's essays, presented by a paid essay coach promoting his own courses; generalizability of 'what worked' from one successful application to other students' situations is inherently limited.
